covalent.note: Covalent radius; PubChem's values are those of Cordero et al., Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832.

vdw.note: Van der Waals radius (Los Alamos National Laboratory).

electronAffinity.note: PubChem lists no electron affinity for this element.

pauling.note: PubChem lists no Pauling electronegativity for this element.

allen.note: Configuration energy (Allen electronegativity) in eV, not converted to the Pauling-like scale; Mann 2000a.

crust.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for Earth's crust, via PubChem ('3.5 milligrams per kilogram').

ocean.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for sea water, via PubChem ('4.5×10⁻¹ milligrams per liter').

solar.note: Proto-solar (4.567 Ga ago) elemental mass fraction, column 'Elemental Mass Fractions' of ESM Table A13; the table gives no uncertainty (relative sigma of N(E) in Table 6 applies).

solarLogEps.note: A(E) = log10(N_E/N_H) + 12, 'Solar System Present' log (E/H)+12; basis: solar value with theoretical considerations; unc = 1 sigma in dex as printed.

body.note: Our table from ICRP Publication 23 has no amount for this element in the reference body (tools/curated/abundance.toml lists what was left out and why).

crystal.note: Low-temperature solid only, at 4.2 K, neutron diffraction. Doubtful: a is given to three significant figures and COD's other ambient-pressure argon entries disagree (Wyckoff 9008462: 5.256 Å at 4.2 K; Dobbs et al. 1956, 1541541: 5.4 Å, no temperature). Check against a modern precision measurement before display.

origin.note: Read off Fig. 39 at the dotted 'age of the Sun' line (t = 9.2 Gyr after the Big Bang, 4.6 Gyr ago): pixel fractions of the stacked areas (agb 0.103, massive_stars 0.556, white_dwarfs 0.342); quantised to 0.05. Stack height 80 px. Cross-check with the paper's text: '34% of Ar ... come from SNe Ia' (figure reading 0.342). Paper: 'For the elements from Ne to Ge, the newly synthesized amounts are very small for AGB stars, and the small green areas are mostly for mass loss.'

gamma.note: Γ/2π from NIST's A_ki = 3.3e+07 s⁻¹ (accuracy class B), taking the upper level to decay only on this line; where it has other decay channels the true linewidth is slightly larger.

laserCooling.note: Cooled in the metastable 4s [3/2]2 (1s5) state; same paper as Kr. first_mot = the paper the Olmschenk catalog lists as first 'laser cooled and trapped'.

biology.note: Not known to be essential for plants or for humans.

history.nameOrigin: From the Greek argos, 'idle' or 'inactive', because it would not combine with anything.
history.symbolNote: Its symbol was A until IUPAC changed it to Ar in 1957.
history.note: Cavendish had noticed an unreactive residue of air in 1785. CIAAW names the discoverer as Robert John Strutt, but the Lord Rayleigh who found argon was his father, John William Strutt.

prose.text: Argon is a colourless noble gas and the third most plentiful gas in dry air; it fills incandescent light bulbs and shields hot metal from oxygen during welding. Its name comes from the Greek for 'lazy', because it reacts with almost nothing. Nearly all of Earth's argon, 99.6 %, is argon-40, built up over billions of years in rocks as radioactive potassium-40 decays; this is why our planet's argon differs from the Sun's, and why argon can be used to date volcanic rocks. The atom's eighteen electrons close the 3p subshell ([Ne] 3s² 3p⁶, ground term ¹S₀).
